strengths: Provides a comprehensive and unifying theoretical framework for expressivity of permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, proving that DWS, NP-NFN, HNP-NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN are expressively equivalent, and that NFT matches them under a general-position (GP) assumption. This resolves ambiguity in a fragmented literature where these architectures were previously studied largely in isolation.

Introduces a clean and well-motivated four-way taxonomy of approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) that meaningfully clarifies what 'expressivity' should mean in weight-space learning, a subtlety not carefully addressed in prior work.

Delivers both positive (universality under GP or with growing architecture) and negative (non-universality in full generality, impossibility for function-space operators under fixed architecture) results, giving a nuanced and complete picture rather than one-sided claims.

Proofs are detailed and mostly self-contained (60+ pages of appendix), with concrete counterexamples (e.g., WL-indistinguishable weight configurations) that ground abstract impossibility claims in clear constructions.
The general-position assumption is natural, measure-zero, and consistent with prior use in the equivariant-network literature, making the universality results practically meaningful.
Identifies real-world relevance for each approximation setting (Figure 2), connecting theory to applications like accuracy prediction, model editing, pruning, and domain adaptation.

The technique of decomposing DWS into a minimal set of primitive update operations (used to also show NFT equivalence) is a nice, potentially useful byproduct that could simplify future architecture design.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical validation, even of claims explicitly framed as testable predictions (e.g., the growing-architecture universality result for function-space operators is acknowledged as unvalidated in the limitations section).

The architectural equivalence results, while technically involved, mainly establish existence of equivalent constructions without addressing efficiency: the depth/width blowup needed for one architecture to simulate another is not analyzed, so practical implications for architecture choice remain unclear.
The universality result for function-space operators requires an unspecified 'sufficiently large' architecture with no quantitative bounds, limiting its practical utility as design guidance.

The general-position assumption, though natural, is noted to break down in realistic settings such as low-precision/quantized weights or symmetric initialization schemes, and the paper only briefly flags this as future work rather than analyzing it.

Significance for practitioners is somewhat abstract; the paper would benefit from at least illustrative empirical experiments (e.g., verifying that a small-architecture DWS model indeed fails to approximate a zoom-out operator, or that a larger architecture recovers it) to make the theory more convincing and impactful.

The individual technical tools used (separation-implies-approximation arguments, DeepSets universality, MLP universal approximation) are largely borrowed from prior work; the contribution is primarily in careful combination and systematization rather than fundamentally new proof techniques.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and previously fragmented gap in the weight-space learning literature by providing a systematic expressivity theory rather than isolated task-specific results (e.g., forward-pass simulation) as in prior work.

The architectural equivalence result (Theorem 5.2, Proposition 5.3) unifying DWS, NP/HNP-NFN, GMN, NG-GNN, and NFT under a general-position condition is a clean and useful organizing contribution that clarifies the landscape of competing architectures.

The four-way approximation taxonomy (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) is a sensible and clarifying framework, and is grounded with realistic use-case examples (Figure 2).

The negative results (Propositions 6.2, 7.1, 7.3) showing failure of universality in full generality, contrasted with the positive general-position/growing-architecture results, give a genuinely informative and non-trivial 'edge case' characterization rather than a purely positive universality claim.

The proofs are detailed and mostly self-contained (extensive appendix with explicit constructions, e.g., cyclic reduction argument for architecture equivalence, canonization map constructions), aiding verifiability.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with zero empirical validation, even for claims explicitly flagged as testable predictions (e.g., that larger input architectures unlock approximation of function-space operators); this makes it hard to assess practical relevance or tightness of the theory.

Many of the core proof techniques are direct imports of existing machinery from adjacent equivariant-network literature (DeepSets universality, canonization-based universality under general position as in sets of symmetric elements/gradient bags, separation-implies-approximation results from Pacini et al.), so the technical novelty is more about careful adaptation than fundamentally new tools.

The results are restricted entirely to MLP weight spaces; extension to CNNs, Transformers, or scale/sign symmetries is explicitly deferred, which limits the immediate significance given that much weight-space learning in practice targets more complex architectures.

The general-position (distinct-bias) assumption, while measure-zero and 'natural', is not carefully examined against common practical settings (e.g., zero bias initialization, weight decay, quantization) beyond a brief remark; the practical prevalence of exclusion-set degeneracies is not empirically characterized despite being central to nearly every positive result.

All results are purely qualitative (existence of approximators) with no discussion of approximation rates, network size/depth trade-offs, or sample complexity, which limits practical takeaways beyond a binary universal/non-universal characterization.

The architecture-equivalence proofs in Appendix D, while thorough, are lengthy and highly mechanical (layer-by-layer simulation across 5+ architectures), which raises concerns about how much new conceptual insight versus bookkeeping is delivered relative to the paper's stated contribution.

strengths: Provides a genuinely unifying theoretical contribution: proves that five prominent permutation-equivariant weight-space architectures (DWS, HNP-NFN, NP-NFN+PE, GMN, NG-GNN) are expressively equivalent, and extends this to NFTs under a mild general-position assumption. The cyclic simulation arguments (Appendix D) are detailed and non-trivial, going well beyond simple restatements of prior 'can simulate a forward pass' results.

Introduces a clean and useful taxonomy of four approximation settings in weight-space learning (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators), which clarifies a previously fragmented literature and gives concrete real-world examples for each setting (Figure 2).

The paper is honest and complete in its characterization: it does not only prove positive universality results but also proves matching negative results (Prop. 6.2, 7.1, 7.3) showing where and why universality fails, and precisely identifies the conditions (general position, sufficiently large output architecture) under which the failures are resolved. This makes the contribution scientifically well-rounded rather than one-sided.

Results have clear practical implications, e.g., explaining why fixed small architectures cannot represent operators that increase geometric/functional complexity (zoom-out INR editing, domain adaptation), and suggesting that larger input architectures can unlock additional expressivity - connecting to broader intuitions about overparameterization.
The writing is generally clear, well organized, and supported by helpful figures (Fig. 1, 3, 4) that make the dense theoretical content easier to follow despite the technical depth.

Extensive appendix with careful, self-contained proofs (continuity of realization map, topological equivalence of function-space topologies, canonization constructions) reflects strong technical rigor.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical; none of the claims (e.g., growing-architecture universality in Theorem 7.2/F.10, or the practical benefit of general position) are empirically validated, even though such validation seems feasible and would strengthen the paper's practical relevance, as acknowledged by the authors.

The scope is restricted to MLP weight spaces with permutation symmetry only; scale/sign-equivariant networks, and weight-space networks for other architectures (CNNs, Transformers), are explicitly excluded, limiting the immediate applicability of the results to the broader weight-space learning literature.

The general-position assumption, while natural and measure-zero in the ambient space, is noted by the authors themselves to be more likely violated in practical low-precision/quantized regimes, which is an important but under-explored caveat given the growing use of quantized models.

The universality results are purely qualitative existence statements; there is no discussion of approximation rates, network size/depth requirements as a function of desired accuracy, or sample complexity, which limits their utility for guiding practical architecture design.

The proofs are extremely long and technically dense (over 40 pages of appendix), making full independent verification difficult for readers; while individual lemmas appear correct and well organized, the overall complexity poses a practical barrier to reproducibility of understanding.

Some central technical tools (e.g., the separation-to-approximation principle used in Theorem 6.1) are imported from very recent, not yet widely vetted preprints (Pacini et al., 2025), introducing a degree of dependency on external results whose own maturity is still being established.

strengths: Unifies a fragmented set of permutation-equivariant weight-space architectures (DWS, NFN, GMN, NG-GNN, NFT) into a single expressivity class via rigorous cyclic-equivalence proofs.

Provides a comprehensive and coherent taxonomy of four approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) with matching positive/negative results for each.

The general-position/exclusion-set framework is reusable and shown to generalize (p-norm exclusion sets, transformer weight spaces in Appendix H), indicating the theory is not narrowly tailored to one definition.
Negative results are proven via explicit, interpretable constructions (e.g., WL-indistinguishable graphs, ReLU linear-region arguments) rather than purely abstract arguments.

Theory directly motivates a simple, broadly applicable architectural modification (OCE) validated with careful ablations isolating capacity effects from parameter count, achieving new SOTA on a standard benchmark even against methods using extra signals.
Includes empirical validation of the general-position assumption under quantization, honestly characterizing where the theoretical assumption breaks down in practice.
Extremely detailed and largely self-contained proofs, aiding reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: Scope restricted to permutation symmetry on MLPs; scale/sign-equivariant networks explicitly excluded, and CNN/RNN weight spaces not treated, making the 'comprehensive theory' claim narrower than the framing suggests.

Empirical evaluation limited to a single benchmark and task type (function-space operators via INR dilation); no experiments validate the theory in the other three approximation settings despite their prominence in the paper.

Some core results (architecture equivalence, forward-pass simulation building blocks) tighten and formalize intuitions already partially present in prior work (e.g., Lim et al. 2023), so novelty is more about completeness/rigor than fundamentally new phenomena in places.

The negative-to-positive narrative for function-space operators (bounded capacity fails, growing capacity fixes it) is a fairly natural/expected result, and the theoretical depth here is comparatively modest relative to other sections.

The link between the capacity-growth theorem and the specific OCE mechanism (parallel ensembling with averaging) is asserted rather than tightly derived, and no alternative capacity-increasing designs are compared.
Several central claims are only stated informally in the main text with full precision deferred to appendices, making it harder to assess exact conditions without consulting supplementary material.

strengths: The paper provides the first comprehensive unification of prior partial expressivity results for weight-space networks, proving equivalence of DWS, NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN (Theorem 5.2), with NFT shown equivalent under a general-position (GP) assumption. This consolidates a fragmented body of prior work into a single expressivity class.

The four-setting approximation framework (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) is a clean and useful conceptual organization of the landscape, illustrated well in Figure 1 and Figure 2 with concrete real-world tasks.

The characterization of when universality holds/fails is precise: universality for function-space functionals in full generality, non-universality for invariant functionals/equivariant operators without GP but recovery under GP, and a clear separation for function-space operators tied to architecture capacity (Theorem 7.2/Proposition 7.1). This gives concrete, falsifiable predictions rather than vague qualitative claims.

The authors go beyond asserting the GP assumption is 'measure zero' and empirically validate it on real pretrained MNIST INRs under varying bias-quantization levels (Appendix G.1), showing GP holds almost surely at standard precision but degrades under aggressive quantization, and further show that combining multiple exclusion sets (Prop. G.3) improves coverage. This is a genuinely useful sanity check connecting the abstract measure-zero argument to practice.

OCE is simple, directly motivated by Theorem 7.2, and produces a meaningful monotonic empirical trend as ensemble size k increases (Table 2), which is consistent with the theoretical claim that fixed output-architecture capacity bottlenecks function-space operator approximation.
Extension to transformer weight spaces (Appendix H) with only minor proof modifications suggests the framework is not narrowly tied to MLPs, strengthening the generality claim.
weaknesses: Empirical validation of the paper's practical relevance rests entirely on a single benchmark (MNIST INR dilation) and a single architectural trick (OCE). For a paper whose abstract and conclusion emphasize 'practical relevance of the theory,' this is a narrow empirical basis; no experiments test the invariant-functional or equivariant-operator universality results (e.g., accuracy prediction, pruning-mask prediction, curvature prediction) that are prominently advertised in Figure 2 as motivating applications.

The comparison table (Table 1) mixes methods that use auxiliary signals unavailable to OCE (gradients in ScaleGMN+GradMetaNet++, probing features in NG-T-64) with OCE's plain weight-only input, making the 'SOTA' and '34% improvement' framing somewhat misleading; the fairer comparison is only against the k=1 same-architecture baselines, which is still a real but much less dramatic improvement.

OCE itself is a fairly simple, almost decorator-level architectural change (widen the output feature/ensemble dimension and average), and its connection to the deep theory (Theorem 7.2) is more suggestive than tightly derived — the theorem guarantees universality via arbitrarily large architectures with a specific partition-of-unity/reference-network construction, not literally via output averaging of k parallel same-size networks, so the empirical mechanism is only loosely justified by the stated theorem.

Large portions of the equivalence proofs (Appendix D) are long, mechanical simulation arguments (constructing explicit layer-by-layer translations between DWS/NP-NFN/GMN/NG-GNN) that, while technically correct, offer limited conceptual insight beyond confirming that sufficiently expressive equivariant/graph architectures can simulate one another — a result perhaps expected given known analogous results in the GNN/DeepSets literature that the paper itself cites.

The GP-based universality results rely heavily on machinery (separation-to-approximation theorems, canonization via bias-sorting) adapted rather directly from existing equivariant-network universality literature (Maron et al. 2020; Pacini et al. 2025a/b; Segol & Lipman 2019), so the degree of originality in the technical machinery, as opposed to its application to the weight-space setting, is moderate.

The paper's claimed practical guidance (e.g., 'applications involving extreme quantization may benefit from more expressive architectures') is stated but not tested with any actual low-precision downstream task or alternative architecture, leaving this as speculation rather than a validated contribution.

Presentation is extremely dense, with the core paper deferring almost all substantive proofs to a very long appendix (60+ pages); while thoroughness is valuable, the main text alone provides limited insight into why the results hold, relying on proof sketches that sometimes gloss over the technical crux (e.g., the sketch for Theorem 6.1 cites an external separation-to-approximation lemma from a concurrent unpublished preprint without much independent justification).

strengths: Fills a genuine and previously under-addressed gap: existing work on weight-space network expressivity was fragmented and task-specific (forward-pass simulation, subsumption results), while this paper provides the first systematic, unifying theory spanning multiple natural approximation settings (function-space functionals, invariant functionals, function-space operators, equivariant operators).

The architectural equivalence result (Theorem 5.2, plus the NFT special case in Prop 5.3) is a strong and non-obvious unifying contribution: it shows that five seemingly different architecture families (DWS, NFN variants, GMN, NG-GNN, and NFT under GP) are provably equi-expressive, which meaningfully consolidates a fragmented literature and justifies treating a 'generic' weight-space network in later analysis.

The four-setting approximation framework is a clean and useful conceptual contribution that clarifies subtleties specific to weight-space learning (the interplay between function-space and weight-space, and between invariance/equivariance), and is grounded with concrete real-world task examples (Fig. 2).

The theoretical results are comprehensive and carefully qualified: the paper proves both positive universality results (under GP or with growing architecture size) and matching negative results/counterexamples (Prop 6.2, 7.1, 7.3, D.21) that sharply delineate the boundary of expressivity, giving the theory real explanatory content rather than only positive claims.

The general-position (GP) assumption is well-motivated, shown to be a measure-zero exclusion set, and importantly is empirically validated on real pretrained MNIST INRs (Appendix G.1), including an informative study of how GP degrades under bias quantization — this substantially strengthens the practical relevance of the GP-conditioned theorems.

The theory directly motivates a simple, broadly applicable architectural modification (OCE) that yields substantial empirical gains (up to 34% over prior SOTA) on a standard INR dilation benchmark with no added parameters, providing a rare and compelling instance of theory-to-practice translation in this literature.
The extension of universality results to transformer weight spaces (Appendix H) demonstrates the framework is not narrowly tied to MLPs and generalizes with only modest technical adaptation.

The technical work is extremely thorough — full proofs (not just sketches) are provided for all major claims in a lengthy, carefully structured appendix, aiding reproducibility of the theoretical results.
weaknesses: Empirical validation of the practical contribution (OCE) is somewhat narrow: results are reported on a single benchmark (MNIST INR dilation) with only two base architectures (DWS, GMN), despite the introduction motivating multiple function-space-operator use cases (domain adaptation, 3D scene editing) that are not empirically tested.

Theorem 7.2 (universal approximation of function-space operators with growing architecture) is existential and gives no guidance on how large the architecture must be in practice, limiting its actionable value beyond motivating the general idea behind OCE.

The claim that prominent architectures are 'equally expressive' is a statement purely about approximation capability with unbounded depth/width, and does not by itself speak to optimization dynamics, sample efficiency, or generalization differences that are known to distinguish these architectures in practice; the paper appropriately flags this as future work, but readers might over-interpret the equivalence result as more practically significant than it is.

The paper is very dense and notation-heavy, even by ICML theory standards; some proof sketches in the main text (e.g., for Theorem 6.3, 7.2) omit details that materially affect understanding of why GP assumptions suffice, requiring heavy reliance on the appendix.

The empirical GP-validation experiment, while a nice addition, is somewhat narrowly scoped (only bias quantization on one architecture/dataset); broader validation across different model families or training regimes (e.g., checking GP violation rates on other public model zoos) would have made the practical-relevance claims more convincing.
